items.title: Cache-aside vs write-through
items.body: In cache-aside the application reads the cache, loads from the database on a miss, and fills the cache. In write-through every write goes to the cache and the database together, so reads are warm but you pay on writes and cache data that may never be read.

source.name: AWS Builders Library - Caching challenges and strategies

items.title: Where to cache in Node, Redis, Postgres
items.question: You have Node.js to Redis to PostgreSQL. Where would you introduce caching and why?
items.answer: Cache-aside in Redis for expensive or hot reads that tolerate brief staleness, keyed by query inputs with a TTL, and invalidated on writes. Add a small in-process LRU in Node only for tiny, very hot, rarely changing data, since each instance holds its own copy. Fix slow queries with indexes first; a cache should not hide them.

source.name: AWS Builders Library - Caching challenges and strategies

items.title: Cache stampede on a hot key
items.question: A popular key expires and 5,000 requests miss at once, all querying the database. How do you prevent this?
items.answer: Let only one request recompute the value (a per-key lock or request coalescing) while others wait or get the stale value. Alternatively refresh early before expiry, probabilistically or in the background, and serve stale on error.

source.name: AWS Builders Library - Caching challenges and strategies

items.title: Add jitter to TTLs
items.body: Keys written together with the same TTL expire together, producing synchronized miss spikes. Adding a random offset, for example a TTL of 600 seconds plus or minus 10 percent, spreads expirations out.

items.title: Why delete the key instead of updating it
items.question: Why do many cache-aside systems delete the cache key after a database write instead of writing the new value into the cache?
items.answer: Two concurrent writers can update the database in one order and the cache in the other, leaving a stale value with no expiry in sight. Deleting forces the next read to load the committed row. Races remain (a slow reader can refill an old value), so still set a TTL as a safety net.

source.name: AWS Builders Library - Caching challenges and strategies

items.title: Why no-cache does not mean do not store
items.question: Why does Cache-Control: no-cache still let browsers store the response?
items.answer: no-cache means a stored response must be revalidated with the origin (for example via ETag and If-None-Match) before reuse. To forbid storage entirely use no-store, which is what sensitive responses need.
